summary: Stateful hash-based signatures like LMS, HSS, XMSS, and XMSS^MT resist large quantum computers, but they must track which one-time keys have been used. This Informational document discusses managing that state and backups safely.

eli5.summary: Each pen works only once, so you must carefully keep track of which pens are used, even if your notebook gets lost.

questions: what is state management for hash signatures
subtitle: Tracking and protecting one-time keys in quantum-resistant signatures

tldr.problem: Stateful hash-based signature schemes are quantum-resistant but require careful management of state to prevent reusing one-time keys, which would allow forgeries.
tldr.mechanism: This document catalogs operational and technical approaches to state management and backup, including multiple keys, sectorization, time-based assignment, and interval-based strategies, along with their trade-offs.
tldr.outcome: Operators have guidance on deploying stateful hash-based signatures safely in constrained environments like firmware signing and IoT, though they remain more complex than stateless alternatives.

facts.label: Key limitation
facts.value: Finite number of signatures per key pair

today: RFC 10033 is an Informational document providing operational guidance for deploying stateful hash-based signatures. It complements specifications like RFC 8391 (XMSS) and RFC 8554 (LMS) by addressing the practical challenges of state and backup management. It is used by organizations deploying post-quantum signatures in constrained environments like firmware signing and IoT.

sections.title: Stateful Hash-Based Signatures and Their Challenge
sections.content:
Stateful Hash-Based Signature Schemes (Stateful HBS) like LMS, HSS, XMSS, and XMSS^MT combine Merkle trees with One-Time Signatures (OTS) to create digital signatures that remain secure even against attacks using large-scale quantum computers. Unlike conventional signature schemes, they depend only on the security of the underlying hash function, making them theoretically very robust.

However, these schemes have a critical constraint: each private key contains a finite set of one-time signature keys, and the state must track which keys have been used. If an attacker obtains signatures for two different messages signed with the same one-time key, they can forge additional valid signatures. This document addresses the operational challenge of managing state and backups safely to prevent this catastrophic failure.
sections.eli5: Some pens only work once before they break. If someone gets two signatures made with the same broken pen, they can fake any signature. So you must never reuse a pen.

sections.title: State and Backup Concepts
sections.content:
Stateful HBS break the private key material into two conceptual parts. The private key is static and long-lived: it is the seed from which the one-time signature keys are derived and does not change. The state is dynamic and mutable: it is a data structure (often a simple counter called an index) that records which one-time key indices have been consumed. The state must be updated on every successful signature.

State management covers mechanisms to securely update state, partition the signature space across multiple devices, transfer unused capacity between devices, and maintain both private key and state backups without risking state reuse. Backup management is a special case: mechanisms to store key and state material outside the signing device, import it to a new device, and recover from failure without rolling back to a state where used keys are available again.
sections.eli5: You keep two kinds of information: the pen instructions (which never change) and a list of which pens you have used. The list must always be up to date. If you lose a notebook, you need a backup, but never go back to an old backup where you have not marked the pens as used.

sections.title: Approaches to State Management
sections.content:
Multiple strategies exist, each with different trade-offs. Multiple Public Keys generates several independent key pairs and keeps secondary keys in storage until the first is exhausted. Distributed Multi-trees uses a hierarchical design where a root tree signs the root nodes of subordinate trees, allowing offline root devices but doubling signature size. Sectorization partitions the signing space into independent sectors with different seeds, allowing parallelization and scaling without increasing signature size.

Other approaches include Key Rotation (generating new keys in sequence), Time-Based State Management (allocating signatures to time windows), and Interval-Based approaches (reserving blocks of signatures in memory). Pre-Assigning States maps signatures to externally ordered objects like software versions, externalizing state management to the application. Each method has implications for complexity, scalability, and resilience to device failure.
sections.eli5: You could have many notebooks (multiple keys), split one notebook into sections for different people (sectorization), or assign pens based on what day it is (time-based). Each way has pros and cons.

sections.title: Deployment Challenges
sections.content:
Deploying stateful hash-based signatures introduces operational complexity unfamiliar to most developers. The selection of appropriate parameter sets (tree height, Winternitz parameters) requires careful design to balance signature speed, size, and key generation time for a specific use case. Organizations must assess operational costs: training staff to prevent state reuse, managing physical media for long-lived backups (10-20+ years), and ensuring backup integrity throughout their lifetime.

Systems need to implement atomic transactions: a signature must not be released before state is committed to durable storage. Hardware Security Modules with rollback-resistant counters are often necessary. Threshold warnings alert operators when signature capacity is running low. Long lifetimes create succession planning challenges to prevent operators from acquiring multiple roles and undermining separation of duties over time.
sections.eli5: Keeping pens organized for decades is hard. Your team must learn the rules. If you lose power halfway through signing, you might use the same pen twice. And you need to remember which pens are gone.

sections.title: Backup and Recovery Strategy
sections.content:
This document proposes a backup strategy for multi-tree systems that extends NIST SP 800-208. After the initial setup, additional subordinate trees are generated one by one and signed by the top-level tree. Each new tree's seed is securely exported, the root node signature is recorded, and the seed is irreversibly deleted from the device. These backups are stored safely.

If all active trees fail (for example, if all hardware modules break simultaneously), operators can initiate one of the backup seeds into a new device, regenerate the tree, and verify correctness by hashing the seed. Signatures from these recovered trees can be combined with the stored root signature to produce valid signatures in the original format. This strategy avoids the single point of failure of root trees and provides recovery paths without rolling back state.
sections.eli5: Before you lose your notebook, you make copies of the pen instructions and store them in a safe place. If disaster strikes, you can start fresh with a copy and never repeat the pens you have already used.
